1.pericope_label: A song in the middle of the judgments: the city made a heap, a strength to the poor

schools.summary: Treat the song as an echo sung from the end of the days, and settle its details textually and typologically: the counsels of old read in apposition, the fallen city both Nineveh or Babylon and the world-power of every age, and the closing word a triumph song rather than a branch.

Explain the interruption psychologically and doctrinally: the prophet takes refuge in praise because he sees the calamities almost before his eyes, and the destruction has its end in conversion, since praise flows only from a sense of goodness.

Set the chapter in its place among the surrounding prophecies, weigh the versions where they differ on number and on strangers or proud, and take the singular city as standing for many with their kingdoms.
Stir up praise by example, hold the eternal counsels and the surprising works together, and read the ruined cities as a lesson that here we have no continuing city.

debates.question: Which city is made a heap?

positions.view: Nineveh, Babylon, Ar of Moab or any fortress of the enemies, the versions disagreeing whether one city or many is meant
the singular put for many, a change of number customary with the prophets
not Samaria or Jerusalem but Babylon, and better still Rome with the antichristian states
Nineveh or Babylon in the prophet's thought, but standing for the world-power of every age, so that this Babylon becomes the type of the later one

debates.question: What is the palace of strangers?

positions.view: read the proud rather than strangers, the two words differing by one easily confused letter and the Greek supporting it
royal cities in which the palaces of Gentiles stood
not foreigners settling in captured towns at all, since it is to be no city, but an ironic picture of highwaymen lodging in palaces because the emptied place has room

debates.question: What is brought low at the end of the fifth verse?

positions.view: the branch, that is the arm or power, a branch being the arm of a tree
the song, a rare noun used so in the Song, the oppressors' triumph song blighting the world until it is hushed

outliers.reading: Alone turns the ruined cities into a meditation on transience rather than on judgment, observing that cities which once flourished in his own nation have gone to decay and are now scarcely known except by urns and coins dug out of the earth, and concluding that we must therefore seek a continuing city to come.

themes: O Lord, thou art my God; I will exalt thee, I will praise thy name; for thou hast done wonderful things; thy counsels of old are faithfulness and truth.
For thou hast made of a city an heap; of a defenced city a ruin: a palace of strangers to be no city; it shall never be built.
Therefore shall the strong people glorify thee, the city of the terrible nations shall fear thee.

For thou hast been a strength to the poor, a strength to the needy in his distress, a refuge from the storm, a shadow from the heat, when the blast of the terrible ones is as a storm against the wall.
Thou shalt bring down the noise of strangers, as the heat in a dry place; even the heat with the shadow of a cloud: the branch of the terrible ones shall be brought low.

6.pericope_label: The feast on the mountain: the veil destroyed and death swallowed up

schools.summary: Read the banquet as the nations admitted to Israel's feast rather than excluded from it, and the veil as both the mourner's covering and the blindness that hides God, with the promise echoing an earlier prophet and re-echoed by Paul and the Apocalypse.

Clear away the readings that make the feast a threat, and refer the whole promise to the reign of Christ from beginning to end, since happiness needs perpetuity and joy together and neither is had in full before the second coming.
Take the feast for the ordinances and comforts given in the church, distinguish the two deaths, and supply the eastern customs that lie behind the covered face and the wine long kept on its lees.
Make the host the point rather than the fare, God preparing as becomes him to give, and treat the swallowing of death as the key that unlocks every other promise here.

debates.question: Is the feast grace or judgment?

positions.view: grace, once two readings are refused: that the Gentiles are invited to prey on the Jews as beasts fattened for slaughter, and that the drink is the cup of wrath
grace, a feast being the usual expression of joy after victory, and confirmed by the unveiling and the abolished death that follow
grace, and characteristically so, the prophet looking to a time when the outlying nations share the feast instead of being shut out

debates.question: What is the covering over all peoples?

positions.view: spiritual blindness and not mourning at all, the veil that lay on Israel's heart
the mourner's covered face, an eastern sign of grief for the dead, so that destroying it defeats death, with the sense of blindness mingled in
the darkness spread by Mahomet and by Rome, and above all the covering of human doctrines and traditions
the Mosaic ritual, unveiled and shown by the apostles to have pointed at one sacrifice
at the resurrection, the bodily death abolished as a penal evil at the cross and finished then
across the whole reign of Christ stretched to the second coming, since we die daily and the chief pillars of the church were treated as sweepings
on an earth already made heaven, the wall between God and the world fallen

outliers.reading: Alone supplies a judicial image for the swallowing of death, the criminal made to drink a cup of poison, which Christ drank instead of a guilty world, and joins to it the Arabian custom of covering the face of the condemned, so that the whole world was being led out to execution when a sacrifice procured a general pardon.

themes: And in this mountain shall the Lord of hosts make unto all people a feast of fat things, a feast of wines on the lees, of fat things full of marrow, of wines on the lees well refined.
And he will destroy in this mountain the face of the covering cast over all people, and the vail that is spread over all nations.
He will swallow up death in victory; and the Lord God will wipe away tears from off all faces; and the rebuke of his people shall he take away from off all the earth: for the Lord hath spoken it.

9.pericope_label: Lo, this is our God: the hand resting on Zion and Moab trodden down

schools.summary: Identify the speakers as the redeemed and account for the abrupt appearance of Moab from the inscriptions, where Chemosh is set against the God of Israel, so that the name becomes representative and even the word for dunghill puns on a Moabite town.

Take the public shout as proof that the grace was actually received, distinguish the hand that rests in assistance from the hand that chastises, and read Moab by synecdoche as every enemy of the church, the nearer kin doing the most damage.
Recover the speakers and the verb from the versions, repoint where the Greek and Coptic support it, and supply the eastern threshing practice that lies behind the treading of the straw.
Hear the cry as the church's welcome and unfold what it contains: the glory passing through the gift to the giver, the recompense for long waiting, and the assurance that he who saved will save on.

debates.question: Who says Lo, this is our God?

positions.view: Jews and Gentiles together, the Greek and Latin reading a plural and the Syriac a second person
the verb is indefinite and best rendered passively, the saying belonging to nobody in particular and to everyone
the redeemed, the citizens of the new city, their supplications turned to anthems

debates.question: What does it mean that the hand of the Lord rests on this mountain?

positions.view: assistance and not chastisement, rest meaning the unbroken continuance of protection where God is worshipped
read rather that the hand shall give rest, repointing the verb on the authority of the Greek and the Coptic

debates.question: Who spreads forth his hands like a swimmer?

positions.view: Moab, thrashing in deep water, the participle better repointed as one who is sinking and the struggle watched by the neighbouring nations
the Lord, whose power Moab can no more resist than water resists a swimmer
the Lord, but noiselessly, since swimmers do not lunge but spread and draw back gently and still cut the water, so that the well-armed are destroyed without armies or uproar

outliers.reading: Alone stops to describe the machine behind the figure, explaining that because meadow and hay are scarce in Palestine and much of the east they chop straw for cattle with heavy iron-toothed wheels drawn over open threshing floors until the stalks are cut to chaff, and that Moab is to be crushed the same way until nothing whole is left in him.

themes: And it shall be said in that day, Lo, this is our God; we have waited for him, and he will save us: this is the Lord; we have waited for him, we will be glad and rejoice in his salvation.
For in this mountain shall the hand of the Lord rest, and Moab shall be trodden down under him, even as straw is trodden down for the dunghill.
And he shall spread forth his hands in the midst of them, as he that swimmeth spreadeth forth his hands to swim: and he shall bring down their pride together with the spoils of their hands.
And the fortress of the high fort of thy walls shall he bring down, lay low, and bring to the ground, even to the dust.
